articleTitle: Introduction to the modelling of wave propagation using TLM
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: Transmission line matrix (TLM) modelling was developed in the early seventies, and the paper by Johns & Beurle (1971) contains most of the concepts required for an understanding of the method. It was first used for the investigation of electromagnetic wave propagation and later for other electronic and electrical problems. It has been applied to a wide variety of wave propagation problems in homogeneous and inhomogeneous media, including electromagnetic compatibility studies of motor vehicles and the modelling of semiconductor lasers. TLM is a method which physically models wave propagation and is ideally suited to simulating sound waves travelling through a medium. In the original work on TLM in electromagnetics, the properties being modelled were voltage and current. The equivalent quantities in acoustics are velocity and either displacement or pressure. The TLM method can be applied in one, two or three dimensions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transmission line matrix modelling applied to thermal diffusion problems (microwave HBT)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: There is currently interest in the use of solid state devices, particularly heterojunction bipolar transistors, (HBTs) for producing pulses of high frequency microwave radiation. The optimal design of such devices necessitates equal consideration of the electrical layout as well as the thermal behaviour. The thermal design process requires the simulation of a repetitive power pulse to ascertain the peak temperature. This may involve simulation over a relatively large time period and use considerable computer time. To try and develop a thermal simulator which was more realistic in terms of its computing requirements it was decided to investigate the transmission line matrix method. The paper outlines some of the features of the TLM simulator which was developed and indicates some aspects of the method which needed to be implemented to develop a potentially useful piece of software. The previous work using finite difference methods had already established that the simulation needed to be three dimensional.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Microscopic effects in TLM heat flow modelling
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: The authors ask some important questions and make one or two apparently outrageous comments. They then outline how they have come to these conclusions and sketch what they believe are the consequences for this type of numerical modelling. Their first comment is probably perfectly obvious and highlights a strength of the technique. One of the wonderful features about transmission line matrix modelling (TLMM) is the fact that one can forget about transmission lines (most of the time). The rules for TLMM of heat flow in homogeneous linear material are simple. There is in fact only the scattering rule, since the mesh forces the subsequent connect process. The scattering coefficients are determined by the transmission line network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The historical development of TLM (transmission line modelling)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: Transmission-line modelling (TLM) is a time-domain, differential numerical technique for simulating electromagnetic and other field problems. The development of the method from the original work by Johns (1971) to the present day is outlined. The emphasis is on setting out the method in its context and bringing out its advantages, limitations and capabilities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling diffusion based processes using TLM
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: Describes the operation of a transmission line matrix (TLM) based model of a diffusion problem. Extension to the basis treatment are reviewed and applications referred to. In TLM both space and time are discretised; the spacial region of interest is divided elemental volumes, and the modelling period is divided into iteration timesteps. TLM is, therefore, primarily a technique of transient analysis. In the diffusion application, TLM not only offers conceptual advantages to many people but can be significantly more efficient computationally than more traditional techniques, since numerical routines based on TLM are explicit, one- step and unconditionally stable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: The application of the transmission line matrix (TLM) to the modelling of electromagnetic field problems is described. A brief description of its basic features starting from simple one-dimensional problem and progressing to more complex three-dimensional problems is presented. Fundamental developments in TLM to deal with losses, nonuniformities and fine features are discussed. The use of multigrid and hybrid nodes is explained followed by a selection of results from a range of applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of TLM in sonar and underwater acoustics
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: Describes a simple model for acoustic wave propagation in water. The model may be used for the analysis of radiation patterns of transducer arrays, beam forming and ray tracing techniques. The paper also introduces a simple model for the analysis of compressional waves in 2D solid structures for transducer design applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of TLM to the modelling of airborne ultrasonics
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: The work described is a part of extensive programme of research into the use of ultrasonic sensors in advanced manufacturing that has been carried out at Nottingham University since 1983. The goal of the programme is the development of a sensor for industrial application which can measure the range in two dimensions of objects within the field of view for both short range (up to 1 mm) and medium range (up to 5 mm). The work involved investigating the TLM modelling technique as a means of simulating the behaviour of ultrasound in air which include testing specific transducer/processing arrangements, feasibility studies of ultrasonic inspection set ups and modelling diffraction or reflection by objects in two dimensions up to far field range. The TLM modelling system used to model sound propagation and its interaction with solid objects in two dimension have been set up on the SUN-SPARC workstation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of TLM-based discrete transforms for general numerical analysis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: The development of a discrete transform based on the transmission line modelling (TLM) method is described. The transform can be used to solve directly by digital computer, electrical networks and other physical problems which can be described by a system of differential equations. The main features of the transform are described including its simplicity, efficiency and stability, and typical results are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of TLM to industrial kiln modelling
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Transmission Line Matrix Modelling - TLM
abstract: The paper concerns itself with on going work on the modelling of a tunnel kiln, allowing the transient nature of heating within the chinaware itself to be investigated and controlled. The model currently incorporates diffusion within the ware, convection and radiation effects. Phase changes within the ware are also being incorporated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
